newsitem.title: CHINA: China military on alert in run-up to HK handover.
newsitem.headline: China military on alert in run-up to HK handover.

text.p: China has placed its three-million-strong army and its police force on high alert against unrest in the run-up to Hong Kong's return to Beijing rule at midnight on June 30, Chinese sources said on Tuesday.

The People's Liberation Army, the paramilitary People's Armed Police, police and security agents have gone on high alert in Beijing and in some other parts of China to guard against ethnic unrest and internal instability, said the sources, who asked not to be identified.
"The authorities are worried the jobless and the democracy movement will create trouble," one source said.

Beijing's communist rulers regard the millions of workers laid off by lumbering state enterprises and China's tiny band of dissidents, most of whom have either been jailed or fled into exile abroad, as threats to stability.
Officials are eager to ensure no domestic unrest ruffles the smooth handover of Hong Kong to China on July 1 after more than 150 years of British colonial rule.

Beijing regards the handover as one of the events of the year -- if not of the century -- for China, and the official China Daily carried a banner headline on Tuesday promising the "Best Welcome Home Party Ever" for the night of the handover.
"They (authorities) are also worried about ethnic separatism," the source said.
The restive northwestern region of Xinjiang has been rocked by pro-separatist rioting and bombings since February.
Riots in the western Xinjiang town of Yining last February left nine people dead and 198 injured. Chinese authorities have executed three of the rioters.

Nine people were killed when home-made bombs planted on public buses blew up within minutes in Xinjiang's capital Urumqi on February 25, coinciding with funeral rites in Beijing for paramount Deng Xiaoping. Eight bombers were executed last May.

In Beijing in March, a bomb exploded on a bus during rush hour in a central shopping district. Chinese sources said at least two people were killed. State-controlled media said no one died but several people were wounded.
Beijing was rocked by at least one other bombing in March, but no casualties were reported.
"The authorities do not want to see another bombing before the handover," another Chinese source said.
The bombings have stunned China's leadership, which has been trying to put on a show of solidarity and stability after Deng's death on February 19.
Plainclothes police patrolling key Beijing streets would be reinforced and police holidays had been cancelled, the sources said.
Late-night patrols of armed police now routinely stop cars, mainly taxis, to check motorists, demanding to see identification papers.

Authorities in the restive Himalayan region of Tibet are also ready to clamp down on ethnic unrest, the sources said. A total of 98 separatists were jailed in Tibet last year for endangering national security.

Beijing police have orders to remove the mentally ill, the jobless, the homeless and beggars from within a one-km (0.6-mile) radius of Tiananmen Square and the Workers' Stadium in the run-up to the handover, sources have said. Handover celebrations are set for both sites.
